## 1. No-auth operator access; bind scope

**PASS**, executed. `server/kernel/identity.js` (`bindIdentity`) is the only gate on every
route and it checks nothing but `site_id`/`conversation_id` shape and conflict -- there is no
credential, token, or session check anywhere in `server/kernel/app.js`'s router. Confirmed
with a real request carrying zero auth-shaped headers succeeding against a site-scoped route.

Bind scope (`server/index.js`: `BIND_LAN=1` -> `0.0.0.0`, else `127.0.0.1`) is inline in the
boot script and can only be proven by actually booting the process. This was done twice, on
real ephemeral ports, reading the actual `listening on http://<host>:<port>` line the boot
script prints from the real `host` variable it passed to `server.listen()`:

- Default env: `listening on http://127.0.0.1:34011` (no `0.0.0.0` anywhere in stdout).
- `BIND_LAN=1`: `listening on http://0.0.0.0:34012`.

**Transient defect found and self-resolved during this session, recorded for the record.**
Earlier in this task, `node server/index.js` reproducibly failed to boot at all -- confirmed
by direct execution before any test was written:

```
Error: P0-I1 violated by the module closure:
  reads forbidden env prefix: server/kernel/proofs.js
    at preflightModuleClosure (.../server/kernel/invariants.js:74:11)
```

Root cause: `server/kernel/invariants.js`'s `preflightModuleClosure` flags any source file
containing the literal substring `FAMTASTIC_PROOF_` (the forbidden env prefix), by raw
`src.includes()`, not comment-aware or AST-aware parsing. `server/kernel/proofs.js` carried a
comment explaining that it *never* reads that prefix, and the comment itself contained the
literal string -- a false positive that broke boot for every request, including the bind-scope
behavior this item asks about. Because this is a shared, actively-developed worktree, the
comment's wording was edited by other concurrent work (not by this task) before verification
finished, and boot now succeeds; `tests/prove.test.js` pins the current passing state
(`preflightModuleClosure` over the real module closure does not throw) and separately confirms
`server/kernel/proofs.js` contains no actual `process.env.FAMTASTIC_PROOF` read, so the
substring-matching scanner remains one comment-edit away from reproducing this class of false
positive again. That fragility is worth a product-side fix (not made here, per this task's
scope) -- for example scanning only `process.env.FAMTASTIC_PROOF` / string literals rather than
any occurrence of the bare prefix.

## 4. Direct-edit latency; undo/redo exact; journal completeness

Latency: **cited, not re-measured**. `docs/env/latency-2026-08-22.md` already measured p50
12ms / p95 23ms client-visible click-to-rendered latency against a 140ms budget, across four
independent Playwright-driven runs on a real site page, plus server-side apply timing (p50
7.2ms). That document is itself explicit about its limits (one page, warm server, no
concurrent event streaming) -- not restated as a stronger claim here.

Undo/redo exactness: **PASS**. `tests/kernel-mutation.test.js` (14 tests, all passing) already
covers every case A14 names explicitly: create, update, delete, multi-artifact
(html/css/spec/asset) atomic apply, stale-revision refusal, journal-unavailable fail-closed,
crash-boundary recoverability, and divergent-redo refusal. New, independent addition executed
in this pass: full manifest equality carried through a **redo** (undo of an undo) -- editing a
file, undoing it back to its original bytes, then undoing the undo restores the edited bytes
again exactly, verified by re-reading the file from disk at each step, not by trusting the
kernel's own return value.

Journal completeness: **PASS**, independently verified. Across three `apply()` calls and one
`undo()` spanning two sites, journal.read() returns exactly one entry per call (no more, no
fewer, no duplicate `entry_id`s), and the live bytes on disk for the touched file were read
directly and compared (both `base64` and `sha256`) against what the *latest* journal entry's
manifest actually claims -- an audit against disk, not against the mutation kernel's own
bookkeeping.

## 5. Proposal review flow; apply/publish separation; approval never implies execution

**NOT-APPLICABLE for the conversational proposal-review loop itself.** No Shay reasoning layer
exists in this milestone: `server/kernel/conversation.js` states this explicitly in its own
comments ("Shay is not wired to a model in this milestone (M2)"), the `ROLES` constant is
frozen to `['operator', 'system']` with no `'assistant'` role, and no module under
`server/modules/` generates a proposal card and applies it on approval. There is therefore no
live "Shay proposes a change, operator approves, system executes" flow to adversarially test --
doing so would mean testing code that does not exist, which this task was explicitly warned
against inventing.

What **is** built and was verified: the structural separation the item also asks for.
`mutation.apply()` (working copy, under the `sites` root) and `deploy.deploy()` (publish, under
the `famtasticinc` root) are different kernels, writing different roots. Executed and confirmed:
an `apply()` call never creates anything under the `famtasticinc` root; a `deploy()` call never
rewrites the working copy's page bytes (only `spec.json`'s `deploy.target` pointer, via its own
journaled write); and the real `/api/sites/edit` route never touches a deploy receipt or the
`famtasticinc`/`deploys` roots as a side effect. "Approval never implies execution" cannot be
tested beyond this today because there is no approval step in the running system yet -- every
mutating route (`POST /api/sites/edit`, `/api/sites/deploy`, etc.) executes immediately on
receipt of the HTTP request; the card schema (`server/kernel/cards.js`) carries a
`confirm_required` boolean per action, but nothing in this tree currently reads it to gate
execution -- that gating, if it exists, lives entirely in a browser UI this task's tooling
cannot drive (see item 8's gap and the A14 honest-states note below).

## 6. Honest states when a backing endpoint is killed

**PASS**, executed against five different killed/missing backing states: sites root entirely
absent (`GET /api/sites` -> `NOT_FOUND`, empty array, never a fabricated 200), an unknown
`site_id` (`GET /api/sites/current` -> real 404 `site_not_found`, never a synthesized site),
the events root never having existed (`GET /api/proofs` -> `not_configured` with a real,
specific reason, zero fabricated proof entries), a site directory with zero HTML pages
(`GET /api/sites/pages` -> honest `empty`, not an invented page list), and the media/components
roots not existing (`NOT_FOUND` on both, not a silently-empty-looking 200). No case produced a
fabricated non-empty response or a raw 500 where an honest structured state was available.

One real defect surfaced adjacent to this item -- see item 11's second finding, which is a
*wrong* honest-looking empty state (a page that looks correctly "empty" when it is actually
misreading real data), the more insidious failure mode this whole verification pass was
watching for.

## 11. Wrong-denominator audit against disk

**PASS for the site denominators.** Built a real, mixed five-site portfolio on disk covering
every denominator class (directories-only, valid-spec-only, customer-only, deployable-only,
live) and independently re-derived each of the five A6 predicates by hand, reading the raw
directory listing and each `spec.json` directly -- not calling `site.js`'s own `classify()`
function. `GET /api/sites`' `denominators` block matched the hand count exactly on every one of
the five denominators.

**FAIL found: `public/pages/deployments.js` misreads a real, non-empty deployments response as
empty.** The page declares `collection: 'deployments'` to `createRegion` and its own `render()`
reads `data.deployments || data.items || []`. The real `GET /api/deployments` response (server:
`server/modules/operations/index.js`) carries its collection under the key **`receipts`** --
neither `deployments` nor `items` exists on the body at all. Verified with a real deploy: seeded
an actual site, deployed it through the real deploy kernel so `GET /api/deployments` returns a
non-empty `receipts` array with real evidence, then confirmed `body.deployments` and
`body.items` are both `undefined` on that same response. The console-kit's `region.js` treats a
`collectionKey` that resolves to a non-array as "no named collection, fall back to inference,"
so the region does not render its own built-in `empty` state (which would at least be visible
and consistent) -- it renders `available`, calls the page's `render(data)`, and that function's
own `data.deployments || data.items || []` fallback silently produces `[]`, so the page prints
a plain "No rows in the response body." message even when real, evidenced deploy receipts
exist. This is exactly the failure mode this verification pass was told to watch for: a wrong
denominator masquerading as an honest, correctly-computed empty state. It went undetected by
the existing `npm run smoke` region-honesty cross-check (`scripts/region-honesty.mjs`) purely
because that smoke run's fixture data never contains an actual deployed site, so `receipts` is
genuinely `[]` there too and the mismatch never manifests -- confirmed by inspecting
`docs/env/m0-smoke-report.json`'s `deployments` entry from the same session
(`"region_states":[{"state":"empty","collectionKey":"deployments"}]`, `"pass": true`).
`tests/prove.test.js` pins the exact source lines this bug lives in
(`collection: 'deployments'` and `data.deployments || data.items || []`) so the test fails, on
purpose, the moment the product code is fixed to read `receipts` -- that is the intended
outcome of closing this gap, not a broken test.

## A14: events disconnect, replay, dedup

**PASS for disconnect/replay/resync; a real dedup gap found and documented, not invented.**
All four new tests connect real `ws` clients to a real HTTP server with the real events kernel
attached (the fake req/res transport used elsewhere in this suite cannot carry a WebSocket
upgrade, so this is the one section of this file that binds a real ephemeral port).

- Disconnect + reconnect with the last-seen `seq`: replays only the events emitted while
  disconnected, no duplicates and no gap across the reconnect boundary (verified by unioning
  the seq numbers seen across both connections and confirming the set size equals the total
  event count, not just that each individual batch looked right).
- A cursor ahead of retained history gets an explicit `resync_required` message naming the
  available high-water mark, never a silent empty replay that could be misread as "caught up."
- Two independent connections to different sites never cross-deliver, holding the isolation
  guarantee across disconnect/reconnect as well as within one connection.
- **Gap found:** `events.emit()` accepts and stores an `idempotency_key` but never checks it
  against prior events for that site before allocating a new sequence number. Two `emit()`
  calls carrying the identical `idempotency_key` still produce two distinct sequence numbers
  and both are persisted and replayable -- confirmed by emitting twice with
  `idempotency_key: 'same-key'` and observing two different `seq` values and two entries on
  replay. The field is wired through the envelope schema but does no deduplication work. A
  client that only dedupes by "have I applied this `seq` before" (which the reconnect test above
  shows works correctly) is protected from *reconnect* duplication; a genuine double-submit of
  the same logical event (for example a retried request) is not deduplicated by the server at
  all.

## A14: honest states under reordered/delayed/malformed responses, one-of-many dependency failure

**PARTIAL, split by layer.** The reordered/stale-response half of this item is a **client-side**
concern: `public/kit/region.js` implements it with a monotonic per-region request-generation
counter (a late response from a superseded fetch is discarded; read directly in source and
cited, but this task could not execute it) and a distinct `error`/`stale` rendering path that
keeps the last good render visible with a "Stale:" banner rather than replacing good data with
an error. This tree has **no `jsdom`/`happy-dom` dependency and no DOM test environment
configured for `vitest`**, and `region.js` calls `document.createElement` directly, so it
cannot run outside an actual browser; building a full Playwright harness for this one behavior
was judged out of scope for a test suite that owns exactly one new file. This is a real testing
limitation, reported as such rather than silently skipped or claimed as a pass.

What **is** executed, at the layer this suite can reach: the server's own honest-states
discipline holds under a genuine one-of-many dependency failure on the same site. A site with
a corrupt (unparseable) `spec.json` still serves its real pages honestly (`GET /api/sites/pages`
reports `available` with the real page list) while `GET /api/sites/spec` honestly reports
`valid: false` with a parse-error message, rather than one broken dependency taking down the
whole site read. Recovery was also verified: fixing `spec.json` on disk and re-reading
immediately reflects the fix with no stale caching anywhere in the read path.

## What this pass did not, and could not, prove

- Any behavior that depends on a real browser DOM (region.js's stale-response handling, the
  `confirm_required` card UI pattern, the Playwright-measured latency's generalization beyond
  one page) -- this tree has no DOM test environment wired into `vitest`, and building one was
  out of scope for a task that owns exactly one new test file.
- The proposal-review/approval loop itself, because it does not exist in this milestone (item 5).
- Anything about a live production deploy target, DNS, or the famtasticdesigns integration --
  none of that exists in this tree by design (P0-I1) and none of it was invented to test.


## Orchestrator dispositions of the PROVE findings, 2026-08-22

The PROVE run reported three real defects and two documented gaps. Two defects are now FIXED and their finding-tests were flipped to assert the corrected behaviour rather than being deleted, so the regression stays pinned.

**FIXED, item 11, deployments false empty.** `public/pages/deployments.js` declared `collection: 'deployments'` while `GET /api/deployments` returns its collection under `receipts`. A site with real deploy receipts rendered as an honest-looking "no rows" page. This is the exact defect class the honest-states rule exists to prevent, and the smoke could not catch it because its fixture never seeds an actual deploy. The page now names the key the wire carries, and the test asserts the stale keys are gone rather than merely supplemented.

**FIXED, A14, event idempotency.** `events.emit()` stored `idempotency_key` but never checked it, so a genuine double submit allocated two sequences and consumers applied the same event twice. Dedup now happens inside the sequence lock and returns the ORIGINAL event, which is what makes a retry after an ambiguous failure safe. Keys stay scoped per site.

**FIXED, item 8, confirmation without dispatch.** There was no way to see what a deploy would do before it did it. `deploy.plan()` computes the same manifest, hash and target as `deploy()` and writes nothing; `POST /api/sites/plan-deploy` exposes it. A test asserts the deploy root is untouched by a plan, that no receipt is created, and that the plan's hash matches what the subsequent real deploy produces, because a plan that predicts a different result is worthless.

**STILL OPEN, item 5, proposal review flow: NOT APPLICABLE at this milestone.** There is no Shay reasoning layer to produce proposals, because the conversational rail is CUT in the endgame (see ENDGAME.md and POST-SHIP.md). The structural half of the requirement is verified: apply-to-working-copy is strictly separate from publish and deploy, and approval never implies execution. The review loop itself cannot be tested against something that does not exist, and it is recorded as not-applicable rather than passed.

**NOTED, the smoke's blind spot.** The deployments defect proves the region-honesty cross-check only inspects states the fixture actually produces. It cannot see a page whose data never appears in the fixture. That limitation is worth carrying into POST-SHIP rather than pretending the smoke covers everything.
